messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol Alvarez is a 38-year-old factory worker who came to treatment nearly two years after her younger brother died suddenly. He had collapsed at work and was taken from the building by ambulance, and by the time Marisol reached the hospital he was already gone. What stays with her is not a broad story of that day but a few piercing details she cannot stop circling back to: the rising siren before she even knew who had been hurt, the terrible stillness of his body when she finally saw him, and the way relatives began speaking in the flat, stunned language people use when a death is too abrupt to understand. Since then, grief-related places and conversations have become charged for her in a way that feels immediate and bodily. A funeral procession passing in traffic, a cemetery she glimpses from a bus window, or a coworker mentioning someone who lost a parent can bring her up short, as if she is back inside the first hours after his death.

In the months after the funeral, Marisol found herself repeatedly trying to solve what could not be solved. When sirens sounded near her apartment or outside the factory, she would lose the thread of whatever she was doing and begin going over the day of his death in exhaustive detail, replaying what time he left home, who called whom, whether there was any missed sign that should have warned them. If a cousin mentioned visiting a grave or a coworker talked about bereavement leave, she would start texting her sister or aunt, asking them to tell her she was okay, that she was not “going crazy,” that other people also got stuck like this. At the same time, she worked hard to push away reminders of loss. She stopped attending memorial masses, avoided driving past the cemetery where her brother was buried, and would leave the break room at the factory if conversation turned toward someone dying or a family funeral. These habits made sense to her as ways to get through the day, especially on a noisy shift where an ambulance on the road outside could unsettle her for hours.

The same moments also began to shape how she saw herself and her future. When the siren of an ambulance cut through the machinery noise at work, she did not just think of her brother; she felt slammed by the conviction that her life had been destroyed and divided into a before and after that could never be repaired. Funerals, cemeteries, even hearing others speak about losing loved ones stirred not only grief but a bleak certainty that the happy version of herself was gone for good. Around extended family she had once felt anchored, but now grief-related gatherings left her feeling separate, almost exiled inside them. Watching others cry together or speak openly about the dead, she had come to believe she no longer belonged anywhere, not among the living people who seemed able to continue and not with the brother she could not stop reaching for in her mind.

Those beliefs, once established, seemed to make the world more saturated with reminders of the death. Because Marisol was certain her life had been ruined and that she no longer fit anywhere, any mention of bereavement in the factory sounded personal, almost accusatory, as if other people were naming what had become of her. On days when she already felt cut off and permanently miserable, the wail of sirens outside the plant seemed louder and more impossible to ignore, and passing a church with funeral cars gathered outside could undo her for the rest of the shift. What frightened her most was how quickly ordinary moments turned into proof that nothing safe or familiar remained.

The things she did to manage this only deepened that hopelessness. Hours of overanalysing never brought an answer, only left her more convinced that her mind was trapped and that the life she had before was unreachable. Each time she sought reassurance from family, the relief was thin and brief; when it faded, she took that as further evidence that something in her had been permanently damaged. Avoiding funerals, cemeteries, and conversations about loss protected her from being overwhelmed in the moment, but it also narrowed her world. She became the one relative who did not show up, the coworker who quietly walked out of the room, and this fed the painful sense that she did not belong even in her own family or workplace.

Marisol finally sought help after leaving her station in tears when sirens passed the factory during a discussion about a coworker’s father dying. She was ashamed that she had again gone straight to calling her sister for reassurance, and afterward sat in her car thinking, with a familiar heaviness, that she was no longer the person she used to be. She comes to treatment afraid that misery is now her permanent state and that any reminder of death will keep pulling her back into the same desperate circling. At the same time, she says quietly that she wants to find some way to hear a siren, or attend a family funeral, without feeling that her whole life is being destroyed all over again.
